title: Known by the one He blesses
hook: He is known by whom He chooses to be known (Sukhmani 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, trai gun: restless, heavy and even calm are weather, and the One is beyond all three. Today, the salok's last phrase, on a fitting day.

Five hundred days. If you've come this far, you've opened this path five hundred times, more than a year's worth of days. You might be tempted to think you've earned something: a level, a closeness, an understanding. And in a way you have. You know words and stories you didn't know. But the sixteenth ashtpadi ends its salok with a line that gently turns the milestone around. Knowing God, it says, isn't something you collect, like miles on a running app.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `HAVE YOU EARNED SOMETHING?` → `NOT MILES ON A RUNNING APP.`

segments.voice: Here's the end of the salok, in paraphrase: Nanak, He makes Himself understood to the one with whom He is pleased. Bujhaae: He causes to understand. Suprasann: well pleased, delighted. So understanding God isn't seized. It's given, by the One, to whomever the One delights in. The Sikh word for that giving is nadar: grace, the glance of favor, literally a look. Japji Sahib puts it in a famous pair: by karma, by your actions, you receive this body like a garment; by nadar, by grace, you find the gate of liberation. Both halves matter. Actions are real and shape your life. But the final door opens from the other side. That can sound unfair, as if effort doesn't count. Sikhs don't read it that way. Look at how the tradition lives: rising early, reciting the banis, serving in the langar, remembering the Name all day. That's a lot of effort. But the effort isn't a payment that buys grace. It's more like opening the curtains. You can't make the sun rise. You can open the curtains every morning, so that when the light comes, it gets in. That's how many Sikhs describe their own daily discipline. The salok's grace is not a wage but a glance, given where the One is pleased. The posture it points to is waiting with the curtains open: not grabbing, and not keeping score.
screen: `BUJHAAE: HE MAKES IT UNDERSTOOD.` · `NADAR: GRACE, A GLANCE.` · `KARMA THE GARMENT, NADAR THE GATE.` · `EFFORT OPENS THE CURTAINS.` · then, large: `KNOWN BY GRACE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up and open, and don't reach for any special feeling. Be like a room with the curtains open in the early morning, ready for whatever light comes and fine if it's still gray. Each time you notice yourself straining, open your hands a little more; if you pray, let Waheguru be the only word, and let even that be quiet.
Nadar, grace, the glance of favor. The One makes Himself understood to whomever He delights in. Effort opens the curtains; nadar is the light.
Your line: known by grace. You can't make the sun rise, but the curtains are yours to open. Day five hundred, with thanks.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of nadar, God's grace, as what finally opens the way, while keeping up daily effort in nitnem, seva and simran; the sixteenth salok of Sukhmani Sahib ends on this note.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nadar, grace, the glance of favor; a word from Persian nazar, sight.

trapdoor: what you thought: if I practice enough, I'll get to know God.
what it means: practice opens you; the knowing itself is given by grace.
what a scholar hears: nadar comes from Persian nazar, glance; Japji pauri 4 sets karmee aavai kaprraa against nadree mokh duaar, and Sukhmani 16 echoes it with bujhaae and suprasann.

chat.says: Five hundred days of practice. Doesn't that earn you a closer bond with God?
options: The salok says understanding is given by grace; practice is like opening the curtains.
Yes, after enough days the closeness is owed to you, like miles on a running app.
No, so effort is pointless; if it's grace, the daily practice doesn't matter.
